title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
titleJa: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
summaryJa: What's gone wrong at Poundland?- Published
bodyOriginal:
What's gone wrong at Poundland?
- Published
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.
Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.
Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.
Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.
How have we got here?
Have people stopped shopping at Poundland?
People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.
Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.
Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.
According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".
She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way".
However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.
So why is it now in administration?
Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer.
However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

- Published10 minutes ago
Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future
- Published1 day ago
It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.
As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.
"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."
Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland.
Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up.
Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on.
Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.
But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.
What's next for Poundland?
Now that the company has entered administration, consultants at Alix Partners have been appointed to pursue a sale of the business and its assets.
There are various options on the table, which include securing a buyer for the business either in whole or piecemeal.
The prime minister has said he wants "every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible".
In the immediate future, Poundland stores and distribution centres will continue operating as normal.

title: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
titleJa: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
summaryJa: The new levies seek to counter foreign trade practices deemed unfair, discriminatory or burdensome to U.S. commerce.
bodyOriginal:
The U.S. is preparing new tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan and India, following investigations into what the Trump administration says are excess manufacturing practices that disadvantage U.S. commerce.
The administration launched those and other trade investigations in March, weeks after the Supreme Court unraveled a major piece of President Donald Trump's tariff-heavy economic policy by striking down his "liberation day" duties. Trump has since been accused by critics of his tariffs of trying to revive the canceled duties using other legal authorities.
The latest action targets foreign economies that create, sustain or contribute to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors that the U.S. finds unreasonable and burdensome or restrictive to its commerce, a senior U.S. official told reporters Tuesday evening.
The new tariffs are "targeted," not blanket rates, and will vary for each economy, and many will not exceed the rates established in previously reached trade deals, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the forthcoming duties.
The rates, which mostly range from 15% to 20%, are "not really additive" and generally will not stack on top of existing duties, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday morning.
"In effect, it'll look more like a top up," Greer said. "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."
An exception is China, which faces a 20% rate under the new tariff policy, "so it will go up some," Greer said. But at the same time, both countries are moving to remove tariffs on some of each other's goods in what Greer called "stability-generating activity through this action."
The senior U.S. official said Tuesday that the 20% rate will come on top of the so-called forced technology transfer-related tariffs of roughly 25%, which were implemented during Trump's first presidential term. U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods will therefore reach about 45%, give or take for different goods, the official said.
Average U.S. tariffs rates on Chinese goods stood at about 36.5% as of July, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Greer also said on CNBC that the new policy likely will not take effect for months.
"We've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing," he said. "I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don't think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now."
The administration says the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" — excess industrial production, often supported by government subsidies, that allows cheaper goods to flood global markets and undercut U.S. producers.
China has disputed the allegations. "The so-called 'overcapacity' does not really exist," China's foreign ministry said Wednesday before the official reports were released by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, according to Reuters.
The overcapacity levies are being imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The Trump administration invoked the same statute to launch investigations into 60 economies over alleged forced-labor issues.
Those investigations, which also began in March, led to broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from dozens of countries covering 99.4% of U.S. imports.
The Section 301 actions came weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs that Trump had enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Shortly after the court's ruling, Trump invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose a 10% global tariff. That tariff expired after 150 days, and was immediately replaced with the forced-labor-related duties.
An ongoing lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of citing forced-labor issues as a "pretext" in pursuit of reviving Trump's worldwide tariff regime.

title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
titleJa: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
summaryJa: The personal consumption expenditures price index was expected to show an annual inflation rate of 3.8% in October, according to the Dow Jones consensus.
bodyOriginal:
Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in the cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal. The reading was 0.1 percentage point higher than September.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.
A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.
Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.
Stock market futures added to losses following the release, while Treasury yields also were sharply lower. Even with the higher-than-expected core inflation figure, expectations eased a bit for Fed rate hikes in 2027. Traders continued to price in two more increases but lowered odds for a third hike to about 1-in-3, compared to 50-50 on Tuesday, according to the CME Group's FedWatch.
"Inflation is too hot and it will not be brought under control as long as economic demand is also too hot," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds.
The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. Less certain is how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.
Inflation had been drifting lower but spiked again following the late-February attacks on Iran led by the U.S. and Israel. Tariffs also have continued to exert pressure, as has strong demand associated with the artificial intelligence buildout. The White House on Wednesday announced a fresh round of tariffs on 14 trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan.
Policymakers generally consider factors such as tariffs and supply shocks to be temporary, but some fear the impact has begun spreading through the economy and could become embedded.
"America's inflation problem is bigger than an energy shock," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.
The large upward increase in GDP came from revisions to investment as well as consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending, which accounts for about two-thirds of all economic activity, rose 4.2% in the third quarter. A metric known as real final sales to private domestic purchasers, which Fed officials regard as a key indicator of underlying demand, jumped 5.8%, reflecting an upward revision of 0.9 percentage point.
In other economic news Wednesday, the Labor Department reported that initial jobless claims slipped to 189,000 for the week ending Nov. 21, down 13,000 from the prior week and back to around the lowest level since the late 1960s. Wall Street had been expecting 200,000.

title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January
titleJa: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January
summaryJa: A household using a typical amount of energy would see its annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.
bodyOriginal:
Energy bills to rise by 26% from January
- Published
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January, under regulator Ofgem's new price cap.
A typical annual bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although individual households costs will depend on how much they use at the coldest time of year.
Ofgem said that, for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales paying by direct debit for gas and electricity, the increase would mean an annual bill would rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if this level was sustained for a year.
The government will make a £100 payment to millions of households from 4 January to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.

title: AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze
titleJa: AI debt worries grow as Nvidia rebound masks Big Tech spending squeeze
summaryJa: Big Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.
bodyOriginal:
Big Tech could find it increasingly tough to secure funding from debt markets critical to the AI build-out, as lenders become pickier over corporate bonds.
Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO on Monday gave an already-rising stock market a further lift, with tech shares leading a broad rebound on Wall Street after last week's sharp sell-off as Anthropic's landmark IPO failed to lift the broader sector.
But investors are now starting to ask harder questions about the bill for the AI build-out — and demanding evidence that the huge spending is actually adding value for shareholders, according to Dan Taylor, deputy chief investment officer and CIO equities, systematic at Man Group.
"As investors get choosier about where all this capital is going and when it might pay off, we think the market is likely to fragment well beyond the simple 'buy chipmakers, sell software' trade of the past two years," Taylor said.
"Anthropic may have got its IPO out the door just in time, but for the rest of the AI trade, the era of spending first and asking questions later seems to be over."
Bearish bond markets
Anthropic — which went public Nov. 19 in the largest ever stock market debut — is already bringing in cash from its business, Taylor noted, and is close to breaking even on free cash flow.
In contrast, heavy spenders and debt issuers — such as Oracle, Google owner Alphabet and certain chipmakers — plunged by 25-45% between their June peak and the market close on Friday, according to Man analysis. By comparison, Apple, which has sat out the AI spending arms race, was up almost 20%, Taylor observed in a Man Group note Tuesday.
Nvidia closed about 5.9% lower on Tuesday. Its shares skyrocketed more than 31% on Monday immediately following Huang's dramatic return as CEO, his reinstatement sparking a huge rally across semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds and boosting equity markets.
Matthew Rees, head of global bond strategies at L&G Asset Management, acknowledged bond markets have been consistently more bearish on Big Tech hyperscalers than equity markets. That stems partly from debt investors' broader outlook on the sector, but also from the sheer volume of issuance, Rees said.
"You're seeing BBB names like Oracle and SpaceX that are trading more like single B, partly because of concerns over fundamental credit quality, but also very much concerns about supply," Rees told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Tuesday.
Accelerated AI-related borrowing is becoming a bigger share of U.S. corporate debt. PIMCO, citing Goldman Sachs data, expects the biggest AI companies to tap about $250 billion through bond sales this year. Across the wider AI industry — including chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — total borrowing could reach $300 billion to $570 billion.
'Not enough money to go round'
Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are now on track to spend more on capital projects than their businesses generated in cash in both 2026 and 2027, according to Man Group analysis. Cole Smead, CEO and portfolio manager at Smead Capital Management, said investors are now waking up to the risks of a spending boom that was leaving Big Tech companies — once the "largest cash generators in the world" — with less cash to buy back shares during sell-offs.
"There are vast capital needs in this AI story. The only problem is there's just not enough money to go around," Smead said.
He also questioned whether investors buying data center debt were being paid enough for the risks they were taking.
"They think they're getting 200-300 basis points over 10-year Treasury," Smead told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" before Huang returned on Monday.
"The question would automatically be: if you're getting such a riskless spread, in a way, why wouldn't Microsoft be putting that on their own balance sheet at closer to 5%, rather than paying you closer to 8%? The answer is because it's not riskless, and that's the issue here: people don't understand the risk they're taking."
Looking ahead, Taylor said the past week has demonstrated that a mega-IPO like Anthropic no longer lifts the whole market.
"We think the mega-cap tech spenders have room to rebound, yet doing so will likely require them to show more spending discipline and rebuild their free cash flow," Taylor said. "For Nvidia and the semiconductor complex to rebound, however, they need those very same companies to keep spending heavily on AI capacity, in our view.
"It is hard to see how both sides get what they need at the same time."

title: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11
titleJa: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund PIF's tower injures 11
summaryJa: This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.
bodyOriginal:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis hit Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund Public Investment Fund Tower on Tuesday, injuring 11.
The kingdom's civil defense directorate did not name the tower, but posted an image showing damage to the PIF tower. Eyewitness reports by Al Jazeera also indicated that the building that was hit was the PIF Tower in Riyadh.
The injured included two Saudi citizens, two Indians, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians.
The attack comes as tensions have flared up again between Saudi Arabia, which is leading an international coalition to restore the internationally recognized government of Yemen after it was forced to flee in 2015, and the Houthis.
Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, said one of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a "cowardly terrorist attack," referring to the financial center in the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
He added that authorities were conducting an on-site investigation at the scene of the attack.
This has been the second attack by the Iran-backed group in six days on the tower, although the previous attack did not cause any casualties.
Red Sea threats
On Wednesday, Houthi brigadier general Yahya Saree warned on X that the port of Jeddah and all Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will become "targets for our forces," if Riyadh attacks the Yemeni Red Sea port of Hodeidah.
The coalition had asked civilians to evacuate the port "for their safety," on Nov. 20.
Attacks by the rebel Houthis have been escalating on Saudi Arabia, with the group targeting one of Saudi Arabia's oil refineries on Sunday, according to Reuters.
The Houthis also launched drone and ballistic missiles against the country's airports, most recently targeting the King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 25, according to reports.
The new attacks come amid wider strikes by Tehran and Iran-linked forces in the Gulf, with Bahrain also reporting that it was attacked by Iran over the weekend. Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.
"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X.
The ministry later said two people, a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.
— CNBC's Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.

title: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
titleJa: Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
summaryJa: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
bodyOriginal:
Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks
- Published
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.
"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.
Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.
The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.
Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?
Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?
At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.
And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.
While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.
"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".
Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.
They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.
State governments could also launch their own investigations.
Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.
"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.
Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.
Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.
In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.
"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.
The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.
The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.
Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.
Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.
The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.
Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.
"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.
"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."
For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.
Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.
He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).
And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.
Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.
He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.
If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.
In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.
Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.
US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.
The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.
Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.
Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.
And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

titleJa: US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
summaryJa: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
bodyOriginal:
US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
- Published
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.
The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
titleJa: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
summaryJa: Once seen as a car for elderly, rural people, tiny cars are being embraced by a younger demographic.
bodyOriginal:
Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
- Published
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.
In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.
He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.
"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."
However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."
These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.
"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.
Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.
Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.
"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.
This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.
"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.
Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.
Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.
"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.
Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.
Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.
"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.
"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."
There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.

title: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
titleJa: What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
summaryJa: Regulator Ofgem is raising the cap affecting the energy bills of millions of households.
bodyOriginal:
What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?
- Published
Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.
The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.
It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.
What is the energy cap and how is it changing?
The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.
It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months, external.
It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.
Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.
The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.
Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.
The typical annual usage figure applies to the first category: dual-fuel households on a standard variable tariff which pay by direct debit.
But customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy used and how they pay for it.
The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs do not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.
Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.
What is a typical household?
Although the price cap sets the unit prices for gas and electricity, your household's actual bill depends on the overall amount of energy you use, and how you pay for it.
Where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.
The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.
The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.
In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.
Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.
Should I take a meter reading when the energy cap changes?
Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.
This is especially important when prices go up.
Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.
Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain
- Published2 days ago
What are standing charges and how are they changing?
Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region, external and payment method.
Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers will be 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.
The electricity charge is lower than the amount charged in the previous three-month period, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.
Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.
The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen
Should I fix my energy prices?
Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.
You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.
Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.
What else has changed about the way energy bills are calculated?
Since 1 April, energy bill charges related to the low-income household insulation scheme - called the Energy Company Obligation - have been scrapped, and for three years, renewable energy projects will be 75%-funded by general taxation instead of a levy on energy bills.
Nearly everyone in England, Wales and Scotland will benefit from this cut, although the amounts will vary between households.
However, the cost of maintaining and strengthening energy network infrastructure like power lines, cables and gas pipes is rising.
In December 2025, Ofgem approved a £28bn investment to improve the electricity and gas grids in Great Britain to strengthen energy supplies and protect customers against volatile energy prices. It will also reduce Britain's dependence on gas.
Customers will pay part of the cost of the upgrade, through an additional £108 added to energy bills by 2031.
These charges started to appear from April 2026, adding about £6 a month to the bill for a typical household covered by the energy cap.
What help can I get with energy bills?
Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.
Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:
Take stock of all household money coming in and going out
Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert to estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate
Tell your supplier if you think you are going to struggle
It is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation
Energy UK has a list of support schemes., external
What is happening to the price of heating oil?
Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.
The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.
In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.
Starmer announces £53m support to help with heating oil costs

title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
titleJa: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
summaryJa: The BBC speaks to three people about steps they take to keep their energy bills under control.
bodyOriginal:
'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
- Published
Domestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.
With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?
The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.
'We power down at peak times'
Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.
The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.
She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.
The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.
To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill.
The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.
They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.
"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.
'We've turned the heating down by 2.5C'
Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.
The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.
Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.
She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.
She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.
"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."
'I order heating oil in bulk'
Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.
"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.
"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."
To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.
Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.
Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.
Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
titleJa: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
summaryJa: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering- Published
bodyOriginal:
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
- Published
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.
During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.
"The RICO count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

title: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
titleJa: Dell earnings beat on AI strength, company authorizes $25 billion buyback
summaryJa: The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.
bodyOriginal:
Dell reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that topped Wall Street expectations for earnings and sales, and provided a strong guide for the fourth quarter.
Dell shares rose in extended trading.
Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates:
- EPS: $9.45, adjusted, versus $6.59 expected
- Revenue: $54.94 billion, versus $49.32 billion expected
Dell said that it expected earnings of $8.40 per share on revenue of about $56.3 billion in the current quarter. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $7.50 per share on $53.61 billion in revenue.
The company's overall sales more than doubled on an annual basis during the third quarter, driven by AI server demand.
The company's largest line is its infrastructure solutions group, or ISG, which makes AI servers and systems, often based around AI chips from companies like Nvidia and AMD.
ISG sales during the quarter were $41.97 billion, topping an LSEG estimate of $35.27 billion. Of that, $22 billion was for AI-optimized servers, up 291% on an annual basis. ISG now accounts for 85% of Dell's total revenue.
"We are now a different company, with Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth," said Jeff Clarke, Dell's vice chairman and COO, in a statement. He said that Dell has 7,500 customers buying AI servers.
In prepared remarks, Clarke said that Dell has a competitive advantage over other computer equipment makers because it allows customers to get their computers working within hours of delivery.
"That allows customers to convert backlog into revenue sooner and more reliably," Clarke said in the prepared remarks published by Dell.
The company also raised its forecast for AI-servers in the coming fiscal year to $78 billion, versus $74 billion expected. The company says it has a backlog of $132.3 billion in AI server orders it is working through.
"Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power," Clarke said on an earnings call with analysts.
The company also sells laptops and PCs, in a group it calls CSG, or client services group. It reported $12.89 billion in sales, which was below LSEG expectations of $14.33 billion.
The overall PC market has been getting whacked of late, with some estimates calling the lull the worst ever, as rising memory prices have led to higher device prices and consumers are choosing to hang on to their old laptops longer.
Dell said that it had authorized $25 billion in share repurchases, and that it had spent $4.9 billion in the third quarter on share repurchases and dividends.
Dell shares are up over 135% so far in 2026.

title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
titleJa: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
summaryJa: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
bodyOriginal:
US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
- Published
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

- Published3 hours ago
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

title: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
titleJa: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
summaryJa: Republicans worry Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affairs with a suspected Chinese spy jeopardized U.S. national security.
bodyOriginal:
President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia. Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.
Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC, the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.
But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."
Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections, as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.
"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."
Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.
"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.
"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.
Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.
There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."
"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.
Republicans ready to probe Huang, Nvidia
Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.
"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.
"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"
Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.
At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.
"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.
Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.
"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security," MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."
Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."
Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk, who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."
But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.
"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.
"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

title: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
titleJa: Drugmaker Insmed shares rally 14% after Sanofi agrees to buy it in pharma’s biggest deal in three years
summaryJa: Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.
bodyOriginal:
Insmed shares rallied 14% on Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.
The proposed acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.
It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff, when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire.
If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.
Insmed shares closed up 14.1% at $170.15 on Tuesday, while Sanofi stock closed up 10.9% in Paris.
'Buys time'
Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside.
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.
Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop toward the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.
Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026, as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026.
While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity.
"Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.
Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA, Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate, following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.

title: Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
titleJa: Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan
summaryJa: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday struck a conciliatory and remorseful tone while leading his first employee meeting since being reinstated, and said how sorry he was for what he had done.
Huang told employees that he let them down and promised to do a better job the second time around, according to people inside the room, who asked not to be named in order to share details. "I hurt all of you," Huang said, according to one of the people.
The CEO also addressed succession planning during the event, the people said. He told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.
A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present.
Investors and analysts were left to speculate about the company's future leadership in the wake of Huang's resignation on Nov. 12.
On Monday, Huang was reinstated as CEO of the chipmaker by Nvidia's board of directors. Eleven days before, Huang had resigned from Nvidia after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said last week that Huang resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
Huang started the meeting by thanking CFO Colette Kress for her leadership as interim CEO.
Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.
In a press release announcing Huang's return on Monday, the company said the board "received input" from senior officials in the federal government about any potential national security risk around the CEO. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and "made the deal" to restore Huang to his post.
After the company had its worst week in the stock market since 2008, the stock surged more than 30% the day his return was announced. Shares fell on Tuesday, however.
An Nvidia representative didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
titleJa: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
summaryJa: Here is what you need to know about the payment that millions will receive from January.
bodyOriginal:
Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
- Published
Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.
Here's what you need to know about the payment.
How much is it?
For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.
A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.
Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.
Will I get the payment? And how can I check?
Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.
As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.
If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.
Will I get it if I live in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland?
The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.
The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.
The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
- Published29 October
How do I get the money? Will I get it if I'm a student or don't pay council tax?
If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.
Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.
The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.
Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.
However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.
Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.
This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.
The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.
Do I have to spend the money on my energy bill?
The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.
But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts so you could choose to spend it on something else, while some people may choose to receive the £100 as a credit on their council tax bill.
How is the government funding this payment?
The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.
The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

title: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
titleJa: Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
summaryJa: There were legitimate fears before Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia - and his return won't fix it
bodyOriginal:
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
- Published
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.
Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.
President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.
In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.
They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.
